title: How to Choose the Best Payroll Provider With HR, Benefits, and Onboarding in 2026
summary: Once a company averages 50 full-time-equivalent employees in a calendar year, it becomes an Applicable Large Employer under the ACA and takes on new health-coverage reporting duties (IRS, checked July 10, 2026). That threshold is one reason payroll, HR, benefits,…
body_text: Once a company averages 50 full-time-equivalent employees in a calendar year, it becomes an Applicable Large Employer under the ACA and takes on new health-coverage reporting duties (IRS, checked July 10, 2026). That threshold is one reason payroll, HR, benefits, and onboarding decisions carry real stakes, and why this guide evaluates nine platforms, Asure included, on the same six criteria. The Decision You're Actually Making This Year You already know you want payroll, HR, benefits, and onboarding running through one system instead of three logins and a spreadsheet reconciling them. The harder question is who operates that system day to day, your own team, or someone else's. That choice sits underneath every provider on this list, even when the marketing doesn't say so. Some platforms assume your team will self-serve every workflow. Others, structured as a PEO, ask you to become a co-employer to get help running payroll and HR. AsureCentral and AsureWorks approach it differently. AsureCentral is Asure's self-service platform for running payroll, HR, benefits, time tracking, and onboarding in one login. AsureWorks is Asure's managed-service alternative, where Asure specialists handle the day-to-day execution on that same platform. There is no co-employment in AsureWorks, you remain the employer of record, and you keep your own choice of benefits, broker, and retirement partners. That makes Asure, through either AsureCentral or AsureWorks, one legitimate path to weigh alongside the eight other platforms this guide covers next, not an afterthought once everything else has been ruled out. Key Benchmarks at a Glance Cross 50 full-time-equivalent employees, and ACA Applicable Large Employer reporting duties begin under the employer shared responsibility rules (IRS, checked July 10, 2026). Publish three per-employee-per-month pricing tiers, Core at $10, Pro at $17, and Elite at $25, with a flat $250 monthly minimum for companies of 25 or fewer employees (BambooHR, accessed July 10, 2026). Payroll itself is sold as a separate, unpriced add-on, and a 15 percent discount applies when bundling payroll with benefits administration for US-based employees. Extend payroll processing to more than 140 countries and territories through ADP's Global Payroll add-on, which integrates with Workforce Now for businesses with international staff (ADP, accessed July 10, 2026). That figure describes the global-payroll integration, not a standalone Workforce Now specification. Require a sales conversation for pricing, with no public per-employee rate listed on Paycor's own pricing page (Paycor, accessed July 10, 2026). Leave G2 or Capterra ratings, review counts, benefits-carrier counts, and implementation-time benchmarks unconfirmed at a primary source for Gusto, ADP, Paycor, Rippling, BambooHR, Paylocity, Namely, and Justworks as of this review. This guide states that gap directly rather than estimating a number. What All in One Means and How These Platforms Were Evaluated For this guide, an all-in-one payroll provider is one where payroll processing, core HR records, benefits administration, and employee onboarding automation all run inside a single login, rather than through a separate onboarding tool or a benefits broker portal that requires its own credentials and a manual data sync between systems. Nine platforms are evaluated here, AsureCentral and AsureWorks together as one entry, plus Gusto, ADP Workforce Now, Paycor, Rippling, BambooHR, Paylocity, Namely, and Justworks, against six criteria: Payroll accuracy and compliance: tax filing handling, multi-state support, and compliance responsiveness. HR module depth: employee records, org management, and reporting capability. Benefits carrier integrations: breadth of benefits administration, self-service enrollment, and ACA compliance support. Onboarding automation: e-signature, new-hire task workflows, and day-one readiness. Pricing transparency: whether per-employee pricing is public or requires a sales call. Implementation time: how long it takes to get payroll live, where a source exists. Each criterion is rated Strong, Moderate, Limited, or Not publicly disclosed. These labels are qualitative judgments grounded in the public evidence available at the time of writing, not a precise numeric formula, and every "Not publicly disclosed" label reflects an honest gap in available data rather than an estimate. Asure's HR Module Depth is rated Moderate here specifically for core HR workflow depth (performance management, learning, succession planning) rather than for platform breadth, where AsureCentral spans payroll, HR, tax, benefits, recruiting, and time in one connected system. Overall Comparison Across All Platforms Provider Payroll Accuracy and Compliance HR Module Depth Benefits Integrations Onboarding Automation Pricing Transparency Implementation Time Asure (AsureCentral or AsureWorks) Strong Moderate Strong Moderate Not publicly disclosed Not publicly disclosed Gusto Strong Limited Moderate Moderate Strong Not publicly disclosed ADP Workforce Now Strong Strong Not publicly disclosed Moderate Limited Limited Paycor Moderate Moderate Not publicly disclosed Moderate Limited Not publicly disclosed Rippling Moderate Moderate Moderate Strong Limited Not publicly disclosed BambooHR Not publicly disclosed Strong Moderate Moderate Strong Not publicly disclosed Paylocity Not publicly disclosed Moderate Moderate Moderate Not publicly disclosed Not publicly disclosed Namely Not publicly disclosed Moderate Not publicly disclosed Moderate Not publicly disclosed Not publicly disclosed Justworks Not publicly disclosed Moderate Strong Moderate Not publicly disclosed Not publicly disclosed Platform by Platform Breakdown 1. Asure (AsureCentral and AsureWorks), Best for Employers Who Want to Choose How the Work Gets Done Best For: Growing SMB and lower-mid-market employers, roughly 10 to 500 employees, that want payroll, HR, benefits, and onboarding on one connected platform, whether they run it themselves or hand routine execution to a managed team. Delivery Model: AsureCentral is Asure's self-service platform. AsureWorks is Asure's managed-service alternative, running on that same underlying system, so a buyer can start self-managed and move to a managed model later without switching platforms. Starting Price: Both AsureCentral and AsureWorks are quote-based, requiring a sales conversation rather than listing public per-employee pricing. Native Onboarding: Yes. AsureCentral consolidates payroll processing, employee records, time tracking, benefits administration, and employee self-service in one login, and onboarding tasks run inside that same environment. HR and Benefits: AsureCentral's benefits administration tools let employees view, manage, and enroll in benefits, and you keep your own choice of benefits, broker, and retirement partners. Asure HR Compliance support helps employers track ACA reporting obligations as headcount approaches the IRS's 50-full-time-equivalent Applicable Large Employer threshold. Key Limitation: Neither AsureCentral nor AsureWorks publishes per-employee pricing publicly, so buyers comparing sticker price alone will need a sales conversation before they can benchmark total cost. AsureWorks provides accountable execution, not a guarantee against every compliance outcome, and statutory liability for the work always stays with the employer. Verdict: For a buyer who wants one platform but hasn't decided who should run it, Asure is one of the few entries on this list where that decision doesn't force a vendor switch later. AsureWorks also functions as a PEO alternative, since the client remains the employer of record and keeps its own choice of benefits, broker, and retirement partners, unlike a co-employment PEO model. 2. Gusto, Best for Small Businesses Wanting Simple Payroll and Benefits Best For: US small businesses, roughly two to 200 employees, running primarily single-state or lightly multi-state W-2 payroll, often through Gusto's accountant and bookkeeper channel. Starting Price: Gusto sells tiered subscription plans (Simple, Plus, Premium), each combining a monthly base fee with a per-person fee, plus separate pricing for Contractor Only and Gusto Global, its international-hiring product. Specific current dollar figures could not be independently confirmed on gusto.com this review cycle. Native Onboarding: Yes, per Gusto's own marketing, though an independent onboarding-automation benchmark was not available this cycle. HR Module: Gusto's HR tools center on core people records and benefits enrollment rather than deep workforce analytics. Key Limitation: Gusto is built for day-one simplicity. Buyers with heavier multi-state complexity or compliance-heavy operations often find it strongest early and thinner as the business scales. Verdict: Gusto rates well on this guide's pricing-transparency and simplicity criteria for straightforward, single-state-leaning payroll and benefits, particularly for buyers who want a tiered, publicly marketed pricing structure rather than a custom quote. 3. ADP Workforce Now, Best for Mid-Market Teams Wanting Broad Compliance Scale Best For: Employers roughly 50 to 999 employees that want a broad, multi-tier product line spanning RUN to enterprise HCM (adp.com), plus organizations that need international payroll reach through ADP's Global Payroll add-on. Starting Price: ADP Workforce Now is typically custom-quoted. Native Onboarding: ADP markets onboarding tools within its Workforce Now tier, though an independent automation-depth score was not confirmed this cycle. HR Module: ADP's HR tools span employee records, reporting, and compliance workflows across a product line that runs from small-business RUN to enterprise HCM. Its Global Payroll add-on, which integrates with Workforce Now, supports payroll in more than 140 countries and territories, according to ADP's own documentation, though that scope describes the global-payroll integration rather than a native Workforce Now specification. Key Limitation: ADP's custom-quote pricing model means buyers need a sales conversation before they can benchmark total cost, and rollout timelines vary based on company size and complexity. Verdict: ADP's advantage is scale and product-line breadth (adp.com) more than pricing transparency or fast rollout. 4. Paycor, Best for Mid-Market Teams Wanting Payroll and HR Analytics Together Best For: Mid-market employers, roughly 50 to 1,000 employees, looking for a packaged payroll and HR suite with reporting layered in. Starting Price: Paycor does not publish per-employee-per-month pricing. Its pricing page requires a sales conversation for a custom quote, according to Paycor's own site accessed July 10, 2026. Native Onboarding: Paycor includes onboarding workflows within its platform, though an independent automation-depth benchmark was not available this cycle. HR Module: An independent, sourced assessment of Paycor's HR module depth was not available this cycle. Key Limitation: The lack of public pricing means buyers cannot benchmark total cost without engaging sales. Verdict: Paycor suits a mid-market buyer prioritizing analytics alongside payroll, provided they're comfortable evaluating cost and support through a direct sales conversation rather than a public price list. 5. Rippling, Best for Fast-Growing Teams Wanting HR, IT, and Payroll in One Record Best For: SMB and mid-market employers, roughly 25 to 2,000 employees, that want to unify HR, payroll, benefits, and device or app provisioning under one employee record. Starting Price: Rippling's pricing is modular, built around a required core platform plus add-on modules, and is often quote-based. Specific per-employee-per-month figures could not be independently confirmed this cycle. Native Onboarding: Yes, spanning HR onboarding and IT provisioning together, according to Rippling's own marketing. HR Module: Rippling's HR tools are built around one employee record shared across payroll, IT, and device management, with a modular structure that lets employers add capabilities as they grow. Key Limitation: The modular pricing structure can make total cost difficult to estimate without scoping each module individually. Verdict: Rippling suits teams that want IT convergence alongside payroll and are prepared to scope modular pricing carefully. 6. BambooHR, Best for HR-First Teams Adding Payroll as a Secondary Need Best For: Employers that treat people management and HR records as the primary need, with payroll as a secondary, add-on priority. Starting Price: BambooHR publishes three per-employee-per-month tiers, Core at $10, Pro at $17, and Elite at $25, with a flat $250 monthly minimum for companies of 25 or fewer employees, according to BambooHR's own pricing page accessed July 10, 2026. Payroll itself is sold as a separate add-on whose price is not publicly listed, and a 15 percent discount applies when bundling payroll with benefits administration for US-based employees. Native Onboarding: BambooHR markets onboarding workflows as a core strength, though an independent automation benchmark was not confirmed this cycle. HR Module: BambooHR launched as a dedicated HR system before adding payroll, and its core plans center on employee records, org management, and people workflows. Key Limitation: Payroll is not included in the base HR plans, so a buyer treating payroll as a co-equal priority needs to price the add-on separately. G2 rating, benefits-carrier count, and implementation time were not independently confirmed for BambooHR this cycle. Verdict: BambooHR is one of the few providers on this list with genuinely public, per-employee pricing for its core HR plans, a real point in its favor for buyers who value pricing transparency, even though payroll pricing stays behind a sales call. 7. Paylocity, Best for Mid-Market Teams Prioritizing Benefits and Employee Engagement Best For: Mid-market employers, generally 100 to 1,000 employees, where benefits strategy and employee engagement sit alongside payroll as priorities. Starting Price: Paylocity's pricing is quote-based. Public per-employee rates could not be independently confirmed this cycle. Native Onboarding: Paylocity markets configurable onboarding workflows, though an independent automation-depth score was not available this cycle. HR Module: Paylocity is positioned in the market as a mid-market HCM platform with benefits administration and employee engagement tools alongside payroll and core HR. Key Limitation: G2 rating, benefits-carrier count, and implementation time were not independently confirmed for Paylocity this cycle, and the absence of public pricing means cost comparisons require a sales conversation. Verdict: Paylocity fits a mid-market buyer whose consolidation priority is benefits and engagement as much as payroll, though buyers should verify current pricing and carrier coverage directly before deciding. 8. Namely, Best for Mid-Market Teams Wanting a Branded Employee Experience Best For: Mid-market employers, roughly 50 to 500 employees, that prioritize a polished, branded, employee-facing HR experience alongside payroll. Starting Price: Namely's pricing is quote-based. A current, confirmed public pricing page could not be located for Namely this cycle. Native Onboarding: Namely markets a branded onboarding portal option, though an independent automation-depth benchmark was not available this cycle. HR Module: Namely is positioned in the market as an HR-first, mid-market platform built around employee self-service and a branded experience layer. Key Limitation: G2 rating, benefits-carrier count, implementation time, and payroll-compliance depth for complex multi-state scenarios were not independently confirmed for Namely this cycle; the comparison table above reflects that gap directly rather than an estimate. Verdict: Namely is worth a look for teams where HR brand and self-service adoption drive the decision, but compliance-heavy payroll needs may call for a more payroll-first evaluation alongside it. 9. Justworks, Best for Small Businesses Wanting PEO-Level Benefits Access Best For: Small businesses, generally under 100 employees, that want access to large-group benefits rates and are comfortable with a co-employment structure to get there. Starting Price: Justworks operates on a PEO pricing model. Current per-employee rates could not be independently confirmed this cycle. Native Onboarding: Justworks markets streamlined onboarding within its PEO model, though an independent automation-depth benchmark was not available this cycle. HR Module: Justworks bundles payroll, HR administration, and compliance support inside its PEO structure, with benefits access pooled across its client base. Key Limitation: As a PEO, Justworks becomes a co-employer of record alongside the client. Buyers who want to keep sole employer-of-record status and choose their own benefits, broker, or retirement partners will find that structure fundamentally different from a managed service such as AsureWorks, which involves no co-employment. G2 rating, benefits-carrier count, and implementation time were not independently confirmed for Justworks this cycle. Verdict: Justworks is the only PEO in this guide, and its case rests on pooled benefits access. Weigh that access against the co-employment tradeoff directly before deciding. Where Each Platform Shows a Documented Strength Support payroll accuracy and compliance most clearly through Gusto, ADP Workforce Now, and Asure, all three rated Strong on this criterion in the comparison table above; Asure's strength here reflects AsureCentral and AsureWorks' native multi-state tax filing, with Asure Payroll Tax Management available as additional specialized infrastructure Asure brings to more complex, higher-volume multi-jurisdiction cases. Show the clearest documented HR module depth through BambooHR and ADP Workforce Now, reflecting their histories as a dedicated HRIS and a broad HCM suite, respectively. Address benefits carrier integrations most directly through AsureCentral's benefits administration tools and Justworks's pooled PEO benefits access, though the two solve the problem in structurally different ways. One preserves the employer's own broker and carrier choices; the other pools access to group rates through co-employment. Rippling and Gusto market onboarding as a core strength, though independent onboarding benchmarks were not available this cycle. Publish the only confirmed, public per-employee pricing among the platforms in this guide through BambooHR and Gusto. Most of the rest, including Asure's AsureCentral and AsureWorks, ADP Workforce Now, Paycor, Rippling, Paylocity, and Namely, require a sales conversation to get a quote. Leave implementation time unconfirmed across every platform in this guide at a verified primary source this cycle. Treat any vendor or aggregator implementation-time claim as unconfirmed until you see it sourced directly. How to Choose Based on Your Company Size and Priority Company Size Primary Priority Consider Why 1 to 49 employees Fast, simple payroll and onboarding Gusto Publishes tiered pricing publicly and is built for straightforward, single-state-leaning payroll. AsureCentral is also quote-eligible at this size for buyers who want payroll, HR, and benefits in one login rather than a payroll-only tool. Under 100 employees Large-group benefits access Justworks PEO model pools benefits access, if co-employment fits your structure 10 to 250 employees One platform, undecided who runs it AsureCentral or AsureWorks Same underlying platform either way, so choosing self-managed or managed later does not require a switch 25 to 250 employees HR-first, payroll secondary BambooHR Built as a dedicated HR system with payroll and benefits available as add-ons 50 to 500 employees Growing compliance exposure near the 50-FTE threshold AsureCentral or AsureWorks with Asure HR Compliance AsureCentral's benefits administration tools and Asure HR Compliance support help track ACA and broader compliance obligations as headcount grows 50 to 1,000 employees HR analytics alongside payroll Paycor Packaged reporting and analytics layered on core payroll 100 to 1,000 employees Benefits strategy and employee engagement Paylocity Positioned in market around benefits administration and engagement tools 25 to 2,000 employees IT and HR convergence Rippling Unifies device and app provisioning with HR, benefits, and payroll 50 to 999 employees Multi-state compliance depth and product-line scale ADP Workforce Now Broad product-line scale spanning RUN to enterprise HCM, with Global Payroll reaching 140+ countries (adp.com, accessed July 10, 2026) Methodology and Sources This guide draws on two categories of information. The first is independently verified public data: the ACA's 50-full-time-equivalent Applicable Large Employer threshold (irs.gov, checked July 10, 2026), BambooHR's published pricing tiers (bamboohr.com, accessed July 10, 2026), ADP's Global Payroll country coverage (adp.com, accessed July 10, 2026), and Paycor's confirmed absence of public pricing (paycor.com, accessed July 10, 2026). The second is Asure's own qualitative analysis of publicly available vendor marketing and documented product scope, applied consistently across all nine entries and labeled Strong, Moderate, Limited, or Not publicly disclosed rather than scored on a numeric scale. Third-party review sentiment (G2, Capterra, and similar sources) was not used as an input to these labels, for any vendor, since that data could not be independently confirmed at a primary source (see below). Several figures commonly cited in payroll-provider comparisons could not be confirmed at a primary source during this review and were deliberately omitted rather than estimated: G2 or Capterra scores, review counts, benefits-carrier counts, and vendor-disclosed implementation times for Gusto, ADP, Paycor, Rippling, BambooHR, Paylocity, Namely, and Justworks; specific per-employee-per-month pricing for Gusto, Rippling, Namely, Paylocity, and Justworks; and any aggregate statistic describing how often SMBs using separate payroll and HR tools experience data-sync errors. Definitions for benefits administration, payroll processing, and employee onboarding automation, as used throughout this guide, follow the plain-language descriptions given under each criterion above. Frequently Asked Questions What does it mean for a payroll provider to be all in one? For this guide, an all-in-one payroll provider is one where payroll processing, core HR records, benefits enrollment, and new-hire onboarding automation all run inside a single login rather than through a separate onboarding tool or benefits broker portal that requires its own credentials and a manual data sync. AsureCentral, Gusto, ADP Workforce Now, Paycor, Rippling, BambooHR, Paylocity, and Namely all fit this definition to varying degrees; Justworks delivers similar scope through a PEO structure rather than a single-employer platform. Which payroll providers publish public per-employee pricing without a sales call? Of the platforms in this guide, BambooHR publishes the clearest tiered per-employee-per-month pricing on its own site, Core at $10, Pro at $17, and Elite at $25 (BambooHR, accessed July 10, 2026), and Gusto also markets tiered subscription pricing publicly. ADP Workforce Now, Paycor, Rippling, Paylocity, Namely, Justworks, and Asure's AsureCentral and AsureWorks all require a sales conversation for a specific quote, based on each provider's own pricing page as of this review. When does ACA compliance reporting start to apply as a company grows? Under the ACA's employer shared responsibility rules, a company becomes an Applicable Large Employer, subject to ACA reporting requirements, once it averages at least 50 full-time employees, including full-time-equivalent employees, in the prior calendar year (IRS, checked July 10, 2026). That threshold is a common trigger point for evaluating benefits-administration and compliance support, including AsureCentral's benefits administration tools and Asure HR Compliance support. Should I run payroll and HR myself, or have it managed for me? That depends on whether your team has the bandwidth and expertise to own payroll, tax filing, and HR administration day to day, or whether you'd rather keep decision authority while handing off routine execution. Asure supports both paths on one platform: AsureCentral for employers who want to run payroll and HR themselves, and AsureWorks for employers who want Asure specialists to handle the operational work, without the co-employment structure of a PEO. Is a PEO the same thing as a managed payroll service? No. A PEO, like Justworks, becomes a co-employer of record alongside the client and typically bundles benefits through its own pooled plans. A managed payroll service such as AsureWorks handles day-to-day payroll and HR execution, but the client remains the sole employer of record and keeps its own choice of benefits, broker, and retirement partners. Your Next Step If you've made it this far, you've probably already ruled out doing nothing. The remaining question is whether your team runs the new platform, or whether you'd rather have Asure's specialists run it for you while you stay the employer of record. AsureCentral gives you payroll, HR, benefits, time tracking, and onboarding in one login if you want to keep the work in-house. AsureWorks gives you the same platform with Asure specialists handling payroll, tax filing, and day-to-day HR administration if you'd rather redirect that time toward the business, without giving up control over your benefits or your people decisions. See how AsureCentral and AsureWorks compare side by side with the other providers in this guide before you sign anything. title: SeaWorld San Diego Debuts a One-of-a-Kind Wonder: Jewels of the Sea – The Ultimate Jellyfish Experience!
summary: SeaWorld San Diego Debuts a One-of-a-Kind Wonder: Jewels of the Sea – The Ultimate Jellyfish Experience! The largest standalone jellyfish exhibit in the country and a must-see in Southern California.
body_text: SAN DIEGO, CA (March 19, 2025) – – SeaWorld San Diego is thrilled to unveil its highly anticipated Jewels of the Sea: The Jellyfish Experience , the largest standalone jellyfish exhibit in the country, is now open to the public. Starting today, visitors are invited to immerse themselves in the mesmerizing world of jellyfish, in this groundbreaking, first-of-its-kind attraction at SeaWorld Parks. Jewels of the Sea showcases the enchanting beauty, fascinating biology, and mysterious allure of these otherworldly animals. Designed to be both captivating and educational, Jewels of the Sea offers visitors a unique opportunity to explore a variety of jellyfish species through engaging, interactive exhibits. The experience features three distinct galleries, each offering a unique perspective on jellyfish and showcasing the variety of jelly species and their locations from the shallow levels of ocean to the deep unknown. Guests begin their journey with an introduction to the fascinating world of jellies, answering key questions about their stings, life cycle, and anatomy. The murals on the walls will guide guests from shallow mangrove forests, where upside-down jellies live, through coral reefs, and into a deep ocean trench, symbolizing deeper exploration. The exhibit opens with nine unique varieties of jellies species displayed through over 15 aquariums. Highlights include one of the largest jellyfish cylinders in the country, a cascading water globe filled with jellyfish, and a fully interactive LED gallery that brings the wonders of the ocean to life. Throughout Jewels of the Sea, the wall corners are rounded to symbolize the flow of ocean currents. The lighting pulses from the arch to the cylinder tank, mimicking the movement of jellies in ocean currents. The exhibit provides a deep dive into the jellyfish life cycle, anatomy, and conservation – one of the key reasons SeaWorld San Diego chose to create this experience. The exhibit also underscores SeaWorld's commitment to marine education and the preservation of ocean ecosystems. In conjunction with the exhibit's grand opening and to highlight the crucial role that jellyfish play in understanding ocean health, SeaWorld partnered with Washed Ashore , a nonprofit organization dedicated to ocean conservation to present a powerful new art installation. Located just outside Jewels of the Sea, the life-sized Lion’s Mane Jellyfish sculpture, made entirely from upcycled marine debris, serves as a striking reminder of the devastating impact of plastic pollution on marine life. Crafted from discarded materials like ropes, plastic bottles, and foam buoys, the sculpture stands as a symbol of the urgent need to reduce waste and protect our oceans. "We’re thrilled to introduce Jewels of the Sea , a one-of-a-kind experience where guests can witness the breathtaking beauty of jellyfish like never before.” said Tyler Carter, Park President of SeaWorld San Diego. “This exhibit not only celebrates these captivating creatures but also highlights their critical role in ocean ecosystems. The Washed Ashore sculpture amplifies the message of ocean conservation and encourages all of us to reflect on how we can help reduce ocean pollution.” “Lion's Mane Jellies are the largest of jellyfish in the world, but their size can't prevent them from the impacts of ocean plastic pollution. Sea creatures of all sizes are being harmed when they mistake microplastics for food or become entangled in this marine debris,” said Brad Parks, Conservation Education Director, Washed Ashore. “We hope this sculpture and all the amazing animals at SeaWorld San Diego inspire every guest to do just one thing to help reduce plastic consumption and pollution, protecting wild places and the wildlife that depends on clean oceans to survive.” To further enhance the experience, SeaWorld is offering the exclusive Jelly Up-Close Tour. This behind-the-scenes journey provides guests with a closer look at SeaWorld’s jellyfish propagation program, along with an opportunity for hands-on interactions with these fascinating creatures in an educational setting. For as low s $11.50, Annual Pass Members can visit Jewels of the Sea endless times with no blockout dates, guests should hurry and purchase now to experience San Diego’s must-see newest attraction. The best way to enjoy this mesmerizing new exhibit is with an Annual Pass , offering: Unlimited visits all year long Exclusive access to seasonal events Complimentary guest tickets during select times No blockout dates Exciting discounts on in-park experiences Don't miss your chance to dive into this one-of-a-kind adventure! Visit SeaWorldSanDiego.com to plan your visit and take advantage of these limited-time savings. Follow SeaWorld San Diego on Facebook and Instagram for the latest park updates and special offers. Events, attractions, and times are subject to change. About SeaWorld SeaWorld is a leading marine life theme park and accredited zoo and aquarium that provides experiences that matter while educating and inspiring guests of all ages to care about marine life. Welcoming millions of guests every year, the parks offer fun and enriching experiences from up-close animal encounters and year-round educational programs to award-winning marine-life-themed rides and attractions, special events, and exciting entertainment. For more than 60 years SeaWorld has advanced the conservation of marine life in and outside its parks through science, education, and exceptional animal care that is Humane Certified by American Humane and accredited by the Alliance of Marine Mammal Parks and Aquariums and the Association of Zoos and Aquariums. SeaWorld is one of the largest marine animal rescue organizations in the world, helping more than 41,000 animals to date. The SeaWorld Conservation Fund, a non-profit foundation established in 2003, has provided more than $20 million to nearly 1,400 organizations to advance critical research on every continent. A portion of park proceeds goes toward supporting these longstanding conservation commitments. SeaWorld parks are in Orlando, San Antonio, San Diego, and Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates (UAE). From Operational Buyer to Agent Supervisor: The Procurement Workforce of the Future Feb 25, 2026 Read more
summary: Lio (formerly known as askLio) builds the world's first AI procurement workforce for enterprise companies worldwide. Every purchase request is managed by specialized agents working in parallel: researching vendors, negotiating terms, managing approvals, and tracking deliveries simultaneously.
body_text: The Three Layers of Tomorrow’s Procurement Department The real disruption isn’t software. It’s structure. Multi-agent systems introduce a new three-layer model for procurement. 01 At the top sits Strategy Communication Leadership and the CPO define sourcing priorities, risk appetite, supplier strategy, governance standards, and performance objectives. → This layer defines what should happen. 02 Strategy Translation is the new role Agent Supervisors convert strategy into operational logic: negotiation parameters, approval rules, risk thresholds, supplier prioritization, escalation triggers, and compliance frameworks. They design and refine Agent Operating Procedures. They don’t execute tasks; they design the system that executes them. → This layer defines how it should happen. 03 Strategy Execution Here, AI agents operate across systems, tools, and stakeholders. They interpret purchase requests, validate suppliers, match documents, conduct operational negotiations, route approvals, and coordinate directly with ERP systems and other agents. Agent-to-agent communication replaces manual coordination loops. Execution becomes always on, scalable, consistent, and data-native. → This layer ensures it actually happens. Together, these layers form a new enterprise architecture: management defines strategy, procurement translates it into operational logic, and agents execute at scale. The competitive advantage will not be the agent. It will be the buyer behind it. Agents follow logic. Humans define it. Operational buyers once checked data, formatted requests, routed approvals, and reconciled mismatches. Tomorrow, they will design agent logic, supervise performance, manage strategic exceptions, and continuously optimize execution systems. The systems remain. The execution layer changes. Procurement doesn’t disappear. It becomes the strategic brain behind an autonomous execution engine.

title: Big names, big matches and big bets: Flutter’s 2026 World Cup wrapped
summary: An epic World Cup has drawn to a close, after more matches than ever before. We look at the breakout teams and the star players that Flutter’s customers bet on.
body_text: Record-setting performances Despite ultimate disappointment for Argentina, this was Messi's tournament and, given his experience and talent, it's unsurprising that he set new records in 2026. He finishes having played more World Cup matches ( 34 ) than any other player, and broke Ronaldo's record as the oldest player to score a World Cup hat-trick. But he was far from the only player to set records. Ronaldo became the first player to score in six consecutive World Cups, and Spain's goalkeeper finally saw his record run of World Cup games without conceding a goal ended at 650 minutes by Belgium's Charles De Ketelaere . Kane became England's leading World Cup scorer, overtaking Gary Lineker, and Mbappé became the Frenchman with the most World Cup matches (21), surpassing Hugo Lloris . One random stat : the 2026 final was the first since 1978 not to feature a Bayern Munich player. Bigger and better? With 48 teams, this World Cup was always going to deliver more goals and more storylines than any before. And growing rumors suggest that the 2030 tournament, to be hosted in Morocco, Portugal and Spain, with early matches in South America, could be expanded yet again to 64 teams. If so, there will be even more chances for the underdogs to win hearts and for the big stars to break records. And, of course, for Flutter's customers to bet on it all.

title: Do AI Auto-Apply Bots Actually Work? LazyApply, Simplify & Sonara: An Honest 2026 Verdict
summary: LazyApply, Simplify, Sonara and other auto-apply bots promise 500 applications while you sleep. Here's the honest, recruiter-side verdict on whether they work.
body_text: Do AI auto-apply bots actually work? Mostly no, and here's the honest reason. Tools like LazyApply, Simplify, Sonara and LoopCV automate the part of a job search that was never really the problem: how fast you can hit submit. They don't fix the part that decides your outcome: are you an obvious match a recruiter can act on in a few seconds? Fire 500 generic applications and you usually just get 500 versions of the same rejection, faster. A tool that autofills forms so you can review and send can save real time. A bot that blasts your resume everywhere while you sleep tends to multiply mismatch, not results. Every few weeks a new post makes the rounds: someone applied to 500 jobs over a weekend using a bot, and they want to know why nothing came back. The number is always big. The response is always small. And the gap between those two things is the whole story of auto-apply tools in 2026. These tools exploded for a reason that has nothing to do with whether they work. The 2026 market is brutal, people are exhausted, and "apply to hundreds of jobs while you sleep" sounds like the answer when you've been ghosted forty times. The appeal is completely understandable. But from the hiring side of the table, what happens to those applications when they land isn't what the marketing promises. This is a fair look at what these bots do, what they don't, and why the thing they speed up is the thing that was never holding you back. What auto-apply bots actually do "Auto-apply" covers a few different products that behave very differently, and lumping them together is where most of the confusion starts. Broadly there are two kinds. The first is an autofill assistant . You build a profile once, and a browser extension pours it into application forms so you're not retyping your work history into Workday for the ninetieth time. Simplify's Copilot is the well-known example here. It autofills across the big applicant tracking systems, Workday and Greenhouse and Lever and iCIMS and the rest, and it can draft answers to job-specific questions from your resume. The key detail: you're still driving. You see each application before it goes. The second kind is a hands-off applier . You set filters, and the tool goes and submits on its own, often on LinkedIn Easy Apply or Indeed or across a pile of boards, until your credits or your daily cap run out. LazyApply is the archetype. It one-clicks the same resume across LinkedIn, Indeed and ZipRecruiter, with no per-job tailoring and no match scoring underneath it. Sonara and LoopCV sit in this family too, along with a crowded field of newer names. Some of the fancier tools bolt an LLM on top to score how well a posting fits you and to generate a tailored resume per job. That sounds like the best of both worlds. In practice the matching is often surface-level, and "tailored" frequently means a keyword-stuffed variant that reads like soup if a human ever opens it. It's worth knowing, too, that a machine-generated resume isn't invisible on the other end; a screen that reads as generated tends to work against you, which is part of why so many resumes get rejected before a human weighs in. One under-discussed mechanic matters here. Plenty of postings force you to create an account before you can apply, which is a big part of what makes the job application process so tedious in the first place. A hands-off bot handles that by spinning up a throwaway account and mailing you a password-reset link later, or it simply skips those jobs because account creation is fiddly to automate. So the "unlimited applications" number quietly excludes a lot of the roles you'd actually want, and includes a lot you wouldn't. Why they exploded in 2026 Desperation is a market. When the manual process feels rigged, anything that promises an edge sells itself. And the manual process genuinely is exhausting right now. Tailor one application, then re-enter the same information into a clunky portal, and you've spent an hour to apply to a single job. Do that all day and you've maybe reached three. Meanwhile you keep reading about people who claim they fired off a hundred a day. The math feels insane, so you reach for a tool that closes the gap. There's a real signal underneath the noise. LinkedIn reported roughly 11,000 job applications submitted every minute on its platform, a 45% jump over the prior year, with generative AI cited as a big driver of the surge. When application volume climbs that fast, part of it is bots. The floodgates are open, and everybody standing in the water can feel it. So the appeal isn't stupid. It's rational, in the narrow way that a tragedy of the commons is rational: every individual doing the thing that maximizes their own odds makes the whole pool worse for everyone, including themselves. The honest verdict: volume was never the bottleneck The whole category gets one thing wrong, and it's the thing that decides everything downstream. Your job search was never limited by how many applications you could physically submit. What limited it was relevance, meaning whether you're a clear, parseable match a recruiter can recognize in the few seconds they spend on your resume before they decide to keep reading or bail. Volume doesn't touch that variable at all, whereas tailoring is aimed straight at it. When you spray a generic resume across 500 openings, you haven't run 500 experiments. You've run the same experiment 500 times, and it fails for the same reason each time: nothing on the page answers the one question the employer is asking, which is why this person for this role. Automating a weak application just gets you a weak application, 500 times over. The people who sift these piles say the same thing again and again: the large majority of applicants to a flooded posting miss the basic qualifications outright, people applying from another country while claiming to live in the States, that sort of thing. So on a req that shows 100 applicants, the qualified minority isn't fighting 400 real rivals. It's fighting maybe a dozen genuine matches, and it wins by being an obvious one. That flips the whole premise. If most of the "competition" is unqualified spray, adding your own spray to the pile is the last thing that helps you. Being the application that visibly belongs is what does. Before you automate a weak resume, find out where it's actually losing. Hiration's free resume review scores how a recruiter and an ATS read your resume, and shows the fixes that make you a match instead of a mismatch. Get your free resume review → The "+100 applicants" illusion Part of what drives the volume panic is that little counter next to a LinkedIn posting. It's misleading, and understanding why takes a lot of the fear out of the game. That number counts people who clicked "apply," not people who submitted something a recruiter would seriously consider. Recruiters routinely note that the visible count is often a small fraction of the real applicant pool, and that when they open a batch of those resumes, the overwhelming majority miss basic requirements: wrong location, wrong seniority, not authorized to work where the job is, no relevant experience at all. LinkedIn even stopped showing the exact figure and switched to "over 100 applicants," partly because the true number was demoralizing people into leaving. So the counter isn't measuring your odds, it's measuring how many people clicked a button, and bots inflate that number without adding a single real candidate to the pool. Apply early when you're genuinely qualified and you're not one of a hundred. You're one of a handful. The badge gets a full breakdown in what "Over 100 applicants" really means . What actually goes wrong when a bot applies for you Beyond the volume fallacy, hands-off appliers create a specific set of problems that show up again and again in real accounts. They apply to the wrong things. Set a bot loose and it will burn through your credits on whatever's in its database that vaguely matches your keywords. People describe getting rejection emails every morning for roles they'd never have touched, in cities they don't live in, at levels they don't want. The tool doesn't check whether you meet the location requirement or the years-of-experience floor or the licensing rule. It sends the CV and moves on. They duplicate. The same job is often posted on three boards, and a bot happily applies to all three. Occasionally that backfires in your favor: the same application hitting an HR rep three times can read as enthusiasm and pull a callback. That's a fluke, not a strategy. More often duplicates just make you look careless. They fill fields with errors at scale. When a machine auto-answers screening questions from a static profile, it gets them wrong sometimes, and you never see it happen. A wrong salary band, a mis-toggled work-authorization answer, a "yes" that should have been a "no." Any one of those can be a silent knockout, and you've now made that mistake across dozens of applications before you notice. The premium spend is real and the value often isn't. These tools are not free at the volume that makes them appealing, and a recurring complaint is paying for a plan, watching it churn through applications with little to show, and then finding the refund harder to get than the signup was. LazyApply, to take one named example, carries a 2.4 out of 5 rating across roughly a hundred Trustpilot reviews as of early 2026, more than half of them one star. It would be unfair to brand any specific product a scam here, because that is a claim no one can responsibly stand behind on the available evidence. What is fair to say is that the reported experience skews negative, and the pattern of complaints clusters exactly where you'd expect: quality, relevance, and refunds. The Sonara lesson: you don't control the tool One more risk gets glossed over: when you hand your job search to a third party, you're trusting a company that might not be there next month. Sonara is the cautionary tale. It was a fully hands-off auto-apply service, the kind that queued and submitted for you. On February 1, 2024 the original service went dark, telling users it hadn't been able to secure the funding to keep running, and people got locked out of their own application queues and history in the middle of an active search. The brand was later bought by BOLD, the company behind Zety and LiveCareer, and relaunched under new ownership. But the lesson stands. If the bot is the one holding the record of where you applied and what you said, its business problems become your problems. The recruiter-side reality: AI applying to AI Now flip to the hiring side, because this is where auto-apply stops being an individual gamble and becomes a systemic mess. A decent posting can now collect a thousand applications by lunchtime, and a large share of those arrive in the first hour, which is a giveaway that they're automated. Hiring managers, especially at small companies without a dedicated recruiter, open their inbox to a wall of resumes from people who mostly never read the job. It's not that recruiters are lazy. It's that the signal-to-noise ratio has cratered, and finding the real candidates in that flood takes far longer than it used to. Employers feel it in the numbers. In a Robert Half survey of more than 2,000 U.S. hiring managers conducted in November 2025 and released in March 2026, 67% said reviewing AI-generated applications had slowed their hiring , one in five reported delays of more than two weeks, and 65% said the surge made it harder to verify whether a candidate's skills were real . That last number is the one that should worry every honest applicant, because it changes how employers respond. And they are responding. The predictable countermove is more friction on the way in: knockout questions, hard qualification gates, and little traps designed to catch bots. One common trick is burying an instruction in the posting, asking you to include a specific word so they know a human read it. Here's the cruel irony, though. Those filters are often trivial for a well-built bot to satisfy and genuinely annoying for a real person to get through. So the arms race escalates, and the humans caught in the middle get squeezed from both sides. The further countermove is a quiet return to the old ways. Some employers are leaning harder on referrals, adding AI screening calls and other verification steps, even bringing back in-person rounds, precisely because a face in a room can't be generated by a prompt. Which quietly rewards the exact opposite of spray-and-pray: being a known, real, verifiable match. Does spray-and-pray ever work? Sometimes, and here's when To be fair, "these tools never work" is too strong, and it isn't true. For roles where you barely need to differentiate yourself, high-volume, entry-level, or no-experience-required jobs, sheer numbers can genuinely pay off. If a posting has almost no bar beyond "can you show up," then there's little to tailor, and applying to fifty of them fast is a defensible move. People have landed those jobs exactly that way, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. The failure is concentrated where tailoring actually matters: competitive roles, experienced hires, anything specialized, anything with a real screen. That's precisely where a generic sprayed application dies, and precisely where most people using these bots are aiming. The tool works worst in the market segment where its users need it most. That's the trap. So the honest verdict isn't "automation is always useless." It's narrower and more useful than that: automate the typing, never the judgment. Autofill so you're not re-entering your address a hundred times, fine. Handing a machine the decision of what you're a fit for, and letting it submit without your eyes on it, is where it goes wrong. What to do instead: fewer, tailored, ATS-clean The alternative isn't "work harder," it's "aim better." The people quietly winning this market aren't the ones with the highest application count. They're applying to ten or fifteen roles they actually fit, tailoring each one, and applying early. A realistic version looks like this. Keep one strong base resume that's genuinely clean for the applicant tracking systems, so it parses correctly and doesn't get mangled before a human ever sees it. If you're building from scratch, an ATS-friendly resume structure is the foundation everything else sits on. If you're not sure it does, that's worth testing, and there are free ways to check whether your resume is ATS-friendly before you rely on it. Then, for each role you truly match, spend fifteen minutes mirroring the language of the posting, not stuffing keywords, but making sure the skills they're asking for are visibly present because you actually have them. Apply within the first day or two of a posting going live, since being early demonstrably helps. And where you can, get a human in the loop, a referral, a direct note to the recruiter, anything that pulls you out of the anonymous pile. That's it. It's less glamorous than "500 applications while you sleep," and it works far better, because it's aimed at the variable that actually decides your outcome. Tailoring is what actually moves you forward. Volume was always a distraction dressed up as a strategy. If your applications keep disappearing into the black hole and you can't tell why, the honest first move isn't a bigger cannon. It's figuring out whether your resume reads as a match at all, then fixing that. A good, tailored, parseable resume beats spray-and-pray on every axis that matters, and it's the one part of this whole broken system you fully control. Frequently Asked Questions Do AI auto-apply bots actually get you interviews? Rarely at the rate the marketing implies. A bot firing off around 500 applications and producing a single callback is a common story, and that one callback often lands only because the tool hit the same job on three boards and the recruiter read it as eagerness. If you're a strong match, ten tailored applications will usually out-perform hundreds of sprayed ones. The bottleneck was never how many you sent. Is LazyApply worth the money? Depends entirely on what you expect from it. LazyApply auto-clicks the same resume across LinkedIn, Indeed and ZipRecruiter with no per-job tailoring, so it's a pure volume play. Its public reviews skew negative, roughly 2.4 out of 5 on Trustpilot in early 2026, with refund and relevance complaints coming up a lot. It isn't a scam, but it's built to maximize speed, which was never the thing standing between you and an interview. What's the difference between Simplify and LazyApply? Simplify's Copilot is an autofill assistant. It pours your saved profile into application forms across the major ATSes so you stop retyping, but you review and send each one. LazyApply is a hands-off blaster that submits on its own until your cap runs out. The first saves you drudgery while you stay in control. The second hands the judgment to a machine, which is where things go sideways. Can using an auto-apply bot get my LinkedIn account banned? It can put your account at risk. LinkedIn's User Agreement and Help pages prohibit third-party bots and extensions that automate activity on the platform, and it uses behavioral detection to catch them. The penalty is a restriction or suspension, not a guaranteed permanent ban, but it's a real exposure, and losing your LinkedIn presence mid-search is a steep price for saving some clicks. Why did I get rejected from jobs I never actually applied to? Because a hands-off tool applied on your behalf. These bots work through whatever's in their database that loosely matches your keywords, so you can wake up to rejection emails for roles in cities you don't live in, at levels you never wanted. It's disorienting, and it's a sign the automation is spending your credits and your reputation on jobs you'd have skipped. If you'd rather stay on top of the roles you actually chose, it's better to apply yourself and follow up on the application deliberately. What does "over 100 applicants" on LinkedIn really mean? Less than it looks like. That counter tallies people who clicked apply, not qualified candidates, and recruiters routinely say the great majority of a flooded pool misses basic requirements. LinkedIn caps the display at "over 100" partly because the true number was scaring people off. If you actually fit the role and apply early, you're competing with a small real pool, not a mob. Is it better to apply to many jobs or tailor a few? Tailor a few, for roles that need any differentiation. The pattern is consistent: a small batch of well-matched, tailored, early applications tends to generate more screens than a flood of generic ones. The exception is high-volume entry-level work where there's little to tailor, and there, speed can win. For anything competitive, quality beats quantity by a wide margin. Do recruiters know I used a bot to apply? Often the fingerprints are obvious. Duplicate submissions to the same company, applications for roles you clearly don't fit, generic answers that don't match the posting, a wave of resumes landing in the first hour, these all read as automated. And whether recruiters can tell you used AI on the resume itself is a related question worth understanding before you lean on any of these tools. Are auto-apply tools making the job market worse for everyone? Yes, and the data backs the frustration. In a Robert Half survey released in March 2026, 67% of hiring managers said AI-generated applications had slowed their hiring and 65% said the flood made candidate skills harder to verify. The predictable result is more filters, more knockout questions, and a slow drift back toward referrals and in-person verification, all of which reward being a real, known match over being a bigger spray. What actually works better than mass-applying? A tailored, ATS-clean resume sent to roles you genuinely fit, early, ideally with a human in the loop. Keep one solid base resume that parses cleanly through the ATS , mirror the posting's real requirements for each application, apply in the first day or two, and reach out to a recruiter or grab a referral where you can. It's less flashy than automating everything, and it's the approach that consistently moves people forward. For the full picture of what happens after you hit submit, it helps to understand how hiring actually works . title: Website Customer Retention Starts With Reasons to Return
summary: Use website customer retention practices to create repeat visits, publish useful educational resources, deliver valuable content, and build stronger relationships online.
body_text: Getting a first visit is only the beginning of a relationship. Website customer retention asks a more useful question: after a person has bought, learned, or contacted you, what good reason do they have to come back? The answer is rarely a louder promotion. It is usually a reliable mix of useful guidance, relevant updates, and an easier next step. Encouraging repeat website visits means treating a returning person as someone with more context, not as a new lead forced through the same introduction. Providing ongoing educational resources gives them progress to make. Building loyalty through valuable content gives them a reason to trust future messages. Together, these actions turn a website into a place that continues to help after the first conversion. Decide what a return visit should accomplish Product Review Feature from Strikingly Website customer retention becomes easier when every important page has a job for the returning visitor. A customer may need setup instructions, a new use case, a care guide, an answer to a support question, or news about an upcoming release. If the website only repeats its original sales pitch, it gives that person little reason to return. A practical return-visit map After purchase: providing ongoing educational resources can help customers use what they chose with confidence. Between decisions: encouraging repeat website visits can surface a timely guide, comparison, or customer story. When needs change: strengthening customer relationships online gives visitors a simple way to ask, update, or explore again. After a useful interaction: building loyalty through valuable content can connect the next resource to a real outcome. Start by reviewing the questions customers ask after a purchase or inquiry. Sales notes, support messages, search terms, and form responses reveal the gaps that matter most. Website customer retention should solve those repeated questions in public whenever the answer can help more than one person. The Strikingly customer-retention guide emphasizes that retaining people depends on the full customer experience, not a single campaign. Do not assume a return means someone is ready to buy again. Encouraging repeat website visits may simply mean helping a person get more value from an earlier choice. That useful, low-pressure interaction is often what makes later business feel natural rather than forced. Build a content library that helps customers advance Providing ongoing educational resources does not mean publishing a stream of generic articles. It means creating a small library around the moments when customers need clarity. Give each resource a clear promise. A guide should help a reader complete something, avoid a mistake, compare an option, or prepare for a conversation. Providing ongoing educational resources works when a person can recognize the benefit before opening the page. It also makes it easier for a team to recommend the right article in an email, a support reply, or a sales follow-up. Use a blog section to group educational work into a durable home, then use blog categories to make related guidance easier to explore. Website customer retention improves when old, useful material remains discoverable instead of being buried by the newest post. Building loyalty through valuable content also requires editorial restraint. Do not publish an article only because a calendar says it is time. Update a useful guide, add a missing example, or answer a new customer question. Website customer retention improves when a visitor can find the right help without remembering its exact title. Add a Site Search option when the library is large enough to need it, and link related resources together. Providing ongoing educational resources becomes easier to use when a guide points toward the next question. Encouraging repeat website visits then feels like progress, while building loyalty through valuable content and strengthening customer relationships online grow from the same helpful path. Make fresh value visible without creating noise Lotus Template from Strikingly Encouraging repeat website visits depends on making new value easy to notice. A returning visitor should not have to hunt through old navigation to discover a new guide, feature, event, or offer. A restrained homepage update, a clear recent-post area, and links from related pages are often enough to signal that there is something worth seeing. Keep the update connected to the visitor's previous interest. Someone who read an implementation guide may appreciate an advanced checklist. Someone who bought a starter product may want a care tip or complementary idea. Building loyalty through valuable content is stronger when the link between the earlier action and the next resource is obvious. Use blog email subscriptions for readers who explicitly want updates, and use Newsletters to share a useful resource with an appropriate audience segment. Providing ongoing educational resources should respect attention: one relevant link is more valuable than a broad, repeated blast. A useful update can also revive a quiet relationship. Strengthening customer relationships online happens when the message recognizes what a person has already done and offers help that fits it. A simple note such as "Here is the checklist for the next stage" is more respectful than pretending every subscriber needs the same introduction. Set a modest rhythm for each audience rather than treating every new post as urgent. Website customer retention can use a monthly resource update, a practical quarterly roundup, and a personal follow-up when a customer asks for help. Encouraging repeat website visits works when the timing reflects a real milestone. Providing ongoing educational resources gives those messages substance, while building loyalty through valuable content makes each contact useful. Strengthening customer relationships online also means allowing customers to choose the topics and frequency that suit them. Use helpful contact points to deepen the relationship Personalized Customer Chat Experience from Strikingly Strengthening customer relationships online is not achieved by hiding every answer behind a form. Make self-service guidance clear first, then give customers an easy way to ask when the issue is personal or complex. A well-designed contact path tells people what happens next and gives the business a chance to learn what the content library should cover. Use a custom form to invite a focused question, feedback request, or resource preference. Use Audience emails for a thoughtful response when someone has already shared their details. Strengthening customer relationships online depends on remembering context and being clear about the next step. Encouraging repeat website visits can also come from light participation. Invite customers to share a result, submit a question for a future guide, or attend a relevant online session. The invitation should match the value already provided. Building loyalty through valuable content means customers feel their experience is useful to the community, not merely useful as a testimonial. Choose one customer milestone that deserves a helpful follow-up. Publish or refresh the resource that answers the next likely question. Link to it from the most relevant page, confirmation, or email. Review the questions and return behavior before planning the next update. Measure whether the relationship is getting stronger Strikingly Store Analytics Website customer retention should be measured with enough context to guide the next improvement. Look at returning visits, engaged reading, resource clicks, subscriptions, repeat inquiries, and repeat purchases where relevant. The number that matters depends on the promise of the page. A support guide may succeed by reducing repeated questions; a resource hub may succeed by bringing readers back at the moment they need help. Built-in Analytics and Google Analytics 4 can identify pages that earn a return or lose attention. Pair that data with direct feedback. Providing ongoing educational resources is successful when customers can describe what became easier, not only when a dashboard reports a pageview. Check the path from a helpful article to the next useful page. If a reader finishes a guide and leaves, add a relevant related resource, a clear contact option, or a next-stage checklist. Encouraging repeat website visits is not about trapping people in more clicks. It is about helping them continue when another step is genuinely useful. Review the library and the relationship every quarter. Website customer retention asks whether customers still find the material timely, whether new questions have appeared, and whether the next action is clear. Providing ongoing educational resources may require retiring an outdated page or expanding a short answer into a guide. Encouraging repeat website visits can reveal which topics deserve a follow-up. Building loyalty through valuable content is reinforced when improvements are visible, and strengthening customer relationships online is reinforced when feedback changes what the business publishes. Keep giving customers a good next reason Website customer retention grows when the website continues to be useful after the first decision. Providing ongoing educational resources gives customers a path forward. Building loyalty through valuable content makes the path feel worth taking. Strengthening customer relationships online makes it possible to listen and respond as needs change. Building loyalty through valuable content gives a team a standard for every update. Strengthening customer relationships online gives customers a voice in that standard. Building loyalty through valuable content and strengthening customer relationships online both improve when every response is specific, timely, and easy to use. Strengthening customer relationships online also means showing customers how their questions shaped the next resource. Choose one customer question that appears often, make the best answer easy to find, and connect it to the next helpful action. Repeat that practice with care. Encouraging repeat website visits will follow when the website consistently helps people make progress.

title: The One Number That Decides Whether Your Restaurant Makes Money
summary: Prime cost is food cost plus labour cost, and it is the single most important number in your restaurant. The formula, the 60% target, and the trap that hides ten points of cost. From an operator who ran 11 restaurants.
body_text: There is a single number that tells you more about your restaurant's health than anything else on your P&L, and most operators have never heard the term. Your accountant probably has, but nobody made it the headline, and that is a shame, because everything else you track rolls up into it. It is called prime cost, and by the time I was 17 I was helping run 11 of my family's restaurants without anyone ever teaching it to me. We tracked food cost when suppliers annoyed us and payroll when it hurt, but we never put the two together, which is like checking each eye separately and never opening both at once. The prime cost formula Prime cost is your food cost percentage plus your labour cost percentage. That is the whole formula. Prime cost % = Food cost % + Labour cost % If your food cost is 32% and your labour cost is 31%, your prime cost is 63%. If you have not run those two inputs recently, my food cost guide walks through the first one in ten minutes, and labour is your total wage bill divided by total revenue. Why does adding two numbers you already know matter so much? Because of what is fighting for the rest of the dollar. Every dollar has four claimants Think about a dollar coming into your till. Four things are fighting for it: food cost, labour cost, overhead, and profit. Overhead is your rent, utilities, insurance and all the fixed stuff, and for most independent restaurants it runs somewhere between 20 and 30 percent of revenue. Here is the uncomfortable part: that slice is essentially locked, because your rent does not go down after a slow Tuesday. Your POS software and card processing sit in that slice too, and unlike rent they are negotiable. I priced out what Square actually costs if you want a benchmark to negotiate against. So profit is what survives after the other three take their share. If your prime cost is 70%, you have somewhere between zero and ten percent left before anything goes wrong, and something always goes wrong. A broken fridge, a slow week, a supplier price rise, and that thin slice is gone. That is why 60% is the target. At 60% prime cost with 25% overhead you are sitting at a 15% profit margin, which is a real business, one that can absorb a bad month, reinvest, and grow. Industry benchmarks back the same line: Restaurant365 puts healthy full-service operations at 60-65% with quick service closer to 55-60%, and Baker Tilly's restaurant practice treats anything sustained above 65% as a margin problem that needs intervention. Every point above 60 comes straight out of your bottom line, not from somewhere else, so a restaurant at 66% is not "a bit high", it is handing over nearly half its potential profit. The trap that hides ten points Now for the part that breaks most operators' numbers, and I say this with love, because I have watched family members do it for years. You are probably not paying yourself properly, and your labour cost looks clean because of it. If you replaced yourself tomorrow, a general manager would cost you $50,000 to $80,000 a year minimum, which is $4,000 to $6,000 a month that is not in your number right now. Add it back in and most owner-operated restaurants jump six to ten points overnight. The restaurant you thought was running 30% labour is actually running 40%, and combined with a food cost drifting toward 40%, you are at 80% of revenue gone before rent gets paid. That is not a restaurant, that is an expensive job you bought yourself. Run your labour cost with a real salary for you in it. That is the honest number, and the honest number is the only one worth managing. Prime cost tells you where the problem lives Here is why this beats staring at food and labour separately: when prime cost is too high, the two inputs point at completely different fixes, and you should not attack both at once. If food is out of range, the work is purchasing, portioning and menu pricing, which I covered in the food cost guide . If labour is out of range, the work is scheduling against your actual cover pattern, cross-training so one person can hold two stations on quiet shifts, and being honest about how much management the building really needs. Put the two percentages next to each other and the guilty one is usually obvious within a minute. Most of the time, the wrong move is the instinctive one: cutting floor staff on your busiest nights. Thin service on a Friday costs you regulars, and as I covered in the money formulas playbook , a regular is worth thousands over their life with you, so saving forty dollars on a shift to lose a three-thousand-dollar relationship is bad maths dressed up as discipline. The labour you can remove without touching service There is one chunk of labour that adds nothing to the guest sitting in front of you, and that is the time your team spends wrestling the phone. Every minute a server spends taking a phone order is a minute they are not at a table, and on busy nights the phone loses anyway, ringing out while everyone is mid-service. So you are paying full service wages for a job that is half done, and the half that gets dropped was holding money. At Baci Trattoria in Naples, Florida, the owner Frank was running five phone lines through his team before he handed the phones to Certus AI's phone agent . The AI has taken more than 1,000 orders and saved his staff over 130 hours that used to disappear into the phone, hours that went back into the dining room, and it recovered over $50,000 in revenue from calls that used to ring out. The full Baci case study has the detail. Notice what that does to prime cost from both ends: labour hours drop without a single person leaving the floor, and recovered phone revenue grows the denominator, which pulls both percentages down together. Certus runs on flat monthly pricing, sets up the same day, and pushes orders straight into Toast, Square, Clover, Skytab, or Aloha NCR. The verdict If you have never calculated prime cost: add this week's food cost percentage to this week's labour percentage tonight, including a real salary for yourself. If the answer starts with a seven, this is now your most urgent project. If you are between 60% and 65%: put food and labour side by side and fix only the one that is out of its lane, then re-run the number in four weeks. If you are at or under 60%: stop cutting and start growing, because at your margins every extra dollar of sales is worth more to you than another point of savings. Full tables and a healthy prime cost are not the same thing, and only one of them shows up in your bank account. Add the two numbers. Want the labour hours your phone is eating back? Book a demo with Certus AI . Twenty minutes, and you will know.

title: MIT Study Reveals That Custom IT Projects Are Hard
summary: The response to MIT’s study showing ‘95% of Enterprise AI projects are failing’ has been one of gleeful schadenfreud for people like me who love soapboxing about how most technology headlines are fake, fraud, or grossly exaggerated.
body_text: The response to MIT’s study showing "95% of Enterprise AI projects are failing" has been one of gleeful schadenfreude for people like me who love soapboxing about how most technology headlines are fake, fraud, or grossly exaggerated. Maybe we missed on the early NVIDIA/PLTR buy, or are jealous of our friends that went to work there in 2018, and so a little headline course-correction soothes those wounds of regret. And while I’d prefer to join the collective flagellation against hype, unfortunately the study‘s focus on "custom enterprise AI build outs" showed me the biggest failure exposed by this study might be the lack of understanding of just how low the survival odds of enterprise IT projects are at large organizations in general, AI or not. In 1994 for instance, surrounded by the buzz of early intranet (and internet) and the dawn of client-server migrations, a measly 9% of ALL large Enterprise IT projects were deemed successful when judged by similar metrics. Three decades later? In 2020, that 91% failure rate dropped to a healthy…90% for large enterprises. Was the hype of "groupware" in 1994 or IoT implementations of 2020 partly to blame for some of that failure? Sure. But less because of the nature of new technology itself and more so because of how we tend to behave in its presence. The constant across incorporating any new technology into an enterprise is the hazardous terrain found when attempting to translate real, solvable business problems into specs, PRDs, and process maps, and then further into solutions with clear roll-out plans, end-user behavior change and adoption. Simply put, any IT project of significance at ANY enterprise of decent scale is far more fraught than we like to think. (Which is why the few software vendors that do repeatably figure out the above pitfalls with productized solutions and predictable experience are able to propagate so quickly.) In 2025, matters are made worse when these hazards are combined with the reality of dealing with non-deterministic language models, exaggerated claims of said models’ performance and top-down project mandates that you should be able to "vibe-code" these successful projects with half the IT resourcing than before. The result, naturally, is a 5% lower success rate. Or, my smooth-brain explanation: that the real new hazard is people writing all those PRDs and specs with ChatGPT. Turning their brains off, spreading gobbledygook and muddy thinking throughout their organizations and onto doomed "Enterprise AI projects." But to get back on my soapbox for a minute… The report did find that vendor-led partnerships were a third more likely to deploy than internally built tools. What’s really holding these ‘AI’ projects back is that these tools don't learn or integrate well into workflows, but when they are actually targeted at specific processes and based on specific outcomes, they can deliver real value.
